## PROP  
 39

## PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### SUMMARY

### Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures

Invalidates mail ballots that do not have last four digits of designated government-issued identification number written on envelope. Prohibits in-person voting without presenting government-issued identification. **Fiscal Impact:** Costs of between tens of millions of dollars and low hundreds of millions of dollars each year to implement new voting requirements. **Supporters:** The Transparency Foundation; Latino American Political Assn; Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Assn; CA Women’s Leadership Assn **Opponents:** ACLU California Action; Common Cause; League of Women Voters of California

### WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS

YES A YES vote on this measure means: Voters would be required to present additional identifying information to elections officials each time they vote.

NO A NO vote on this measure means: A voter’s identity would continue to be established with the voter’s signature.

 

### ARGUMENTS

PRO Yes on Prop. 39 gives California a BIPARTISAN solution for VOTER ID. Supported by a solid majority of Democratic, Independent and Republican voters. Increases trust and confidence in our elections.

CON No on Prop. 39. This would advance Trump’s voter suppression agenda by adding costly, unnecessary barriers that could block eligible California voters, expose personal information to identity theft, and waste hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars. Don’t let MAGA billionaires decide which voters count. Vote No.

## PROP  
 39

## PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

## ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST

### BACKGROUND

***Elections Administration.*** County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have workload related to voting. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state *Voter Information Guide*.

***United States Citizenship Required to Vote in Federal, State, and Almost All Local Elections*** A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in any state or federal election. A noncitizen who votes in a state or federal election can be fined and/or sentenced to prison. A person must be a U.S. citizen to vote in the vast majority of local elections. (San Francisco and Oakland have a special process for people who are not U.S. citizens to vote only in school board elections if they are the parent, guardian, or legally recognized caregiver of a student in the school district.)

***Voter Registration.*** In order to vote, people first must register with elections officials. People register to vote in the county where they live. To be eligible to register, a person must be a U.S. citizen, live in California, be at least 18 years old, not currently be in prison, and not be found unable to vote by a court. A person who makes a false statement when attempting to register to vote in California, such as by falsely stating that they are a U.S. citizen, is guilty of the crime of perjury. People can register online through the Secretary of State’s website, by mail, in person at a county elections office, or through the California Department of Motor Vehicles. A voter’s identity is established through the registration process by using their driver’s license number, state identification number, or last four digits of their Social Security number. Voters who do not provide this identifying information through the registration process may be asked to present identification the first time they vote.

***Voter Rolls Maintenance.*** A voter roll is a list of people who are registered to vote. Elections officials are required to keep the voter rolls up to date by removing people who are no longer eligible to vote from the list. For example, elections officials receive regular updates from other government entities to identify people who have died or are in prison.

***Voting.*** All registered voters in California receive a vote by mail (VBM) ballot. Voters can mail their ballot, drop it off at a ballot drop-off location, or vote in person at a voting location. In the November 2024 Presidential Election, about 16 million people voted in California. About 13 million voted using a VBM ballot, and about 3 million voted in person.

***Voter Identification.*** Voters identify themselves when they vote in California. If they vote in person, they typically identify themselves by signing a list of registered voters before voting. If they vote by mail, they identify themselves by signing the envelope of their ballot. Elections officials verify signatures for VBM ballots before counting them. Elections officials generally do not verify signatures from in-person voters before counting the ballots.

***California State Auditor’s Office (State Auditor).*** The State Auditor is an independent and nonpartisan office in state government. It reviews how well the state and local governments use money and run their programs. These reviews include performance audits to see if the government is following the law and working efficiently. The State Auditor may give recommendations to help improve government operations and efficiency. Some audits happen regularly, while others are done only once.

### PROPOSAL

***Requires State and Local Elections Officials to Verify U.S. Citizenship Status of Registered Voters.*** Proposition 39 requires state and local elections officials to make “best efforts” using government data to verify that voters on the rolls are U.S. citizens. Proposition 39 requires elections officials to report every year the percentage of registered voters in each county whose citizenship status has been verified.

***Requires Voters to Select Government- Issued Identification for Voting by Mail.*** Proposition 39 requires new and existing voters to select a government-issued identification in their voter registration to vote by mail.

***Requires Voters to Provide Additional Identifying Information to Vote.*** Proposition 39 requires voters to provide additional identifying information each time they cast a ballot in any election in California. Elections officials would be required to verify voters’ identities before counting their ballots. The identification requirement would depend on whether a voter casts their ballot in person or by mail: 

*   ***In-Person Voting.*** When voting in person, Proposition 39 requires voters to present government-issued identification for identity verification.
*   ***Voting by Mail.*** When voting by mail, Proposition 39 requires voters to provide the last four digits of their selected government-issued identification number on the ballot envelope. Elections officials would verify that the identification numbers provided on the ballot envelope match the voter’s registration information.

***Creates New State-Issued Voter Identification Card.*** Proposition 39 requires the state to provide a voter identification card at no cost to voters who request one. The voter identification card could be used as the government-issued identification that verifies a voter’s identity when voting.

***Requires State Auditor to Audit State and County Election Compliance Regularly.*** In every odd-numbered year, Proposition 39 requires the State Auditor to report how well the state and each county comply with the measure and make recommendations for improvement.

***Requires Legislative Action for Full Implementation.*** Proposition 39 requires the Legislature to pass additional laws to implement the measure. The Legislature would need to clarify several details that are not defined in the proposition, like which forms of identification could be used and what steps would be considered best efforts to verify the citizenship status of registered voters.

### FISCAL EFFECTS

***State and Local Costs Depend on Future Decisions.*** Proposition 39 would increase state and local government costs each year by **tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars**. These costs represent less than one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) The exact cost would depend on future choices made by the Legislature, state departments, local governments, and voters. For example, the costs could vary depending on decisions around the design and requirements of the voter identification card and the number of cards requested. There also could be some amount of savings. These savings would be due to fewer people registered to vote—for example, due to the removal of ineligible voters or eligible voters lacking government-issued identification. These savings likely would not exceed the costs of the measure.

## PROP  
 39

## PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.

### ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39

*VOTER ID: A BIPARTISAN WAY TO INCREASE TRUST IN OUR ELECTIONS*

Democratic, Independent, and Republican voters all agree on one thing: Voter ID is a common-sense reform to increase trust and participation in our elections. That’s why almost half the signatures to put Prop. 39 on the ballot came from Democratic and Independent voters and polls show widespread super-majority support across all political parties for Voter ID.

*PROP. 39 KEEPS VOTING ACCESSIBLE AND GUARANTEES A FREE VOTER ID*

Prop. 39 keeps mail ballots, extended polling hours and all other conveniences in place for voting accessibility.

Voters can use a variety of easily-obtained government IDs to vote—and this measure even guarantees every voter a FREE Voter ID if they want one.

California currently uses a slow process to check signatures on mail ballots that not only delays election results but also puts your vote at risk of not being counted if your signature is flagged as not matching. Many voters say they cannot always remember how they signed their name years ago when they first registered to vote. In the last election, more than 100,000 ballots were rejected due to signature mismatches—and more than 200,000 voters endured hassles just to get their vote to count.

*VOTER ID INCREASES PARTICIPATION*

Voter ID does not suppress voting—in fact it increases voter participation. Every state with Voter ID laws and free identification for eligible voters that cannot afford or access identification, has seen an increase in voting. Suppression and lower turnout happen when voters do not have trust and confidence in the integrity of the process. Voter ID gives all voters a reason to trust that their vote will matter.

*PROP. 39 INCLUDES AUDITS AND CITIZENSHIP VERIFICATION*

Prop. 39 holds election officials accountable for keeping California’s voter lists accurate and updated. Election officials will also be required to check voter rolls to ensure only citizens are registered. Prop. 39 requires an independent audit be conducted every two years to give the public the confidence they deserve in the way our elections are conducted.

*YES ON PROP. 39: FOR A NON-PARTISAN SOLUTION TO VOTER ID*

Politicians and partisan organizations who oppose Prop. 39 are desperately trying to inject toxic partisanship into this debate. That’s because they benefit from unfounded election conspiracy theories and rapidly declining trust in our elections.

In contrast, supporters of Prop. 39 include solid majorities of Democratic, Republican and Independent voters and a diverse coalition including Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, the Transparency Foundation, and trusted voting rights organizations. Vote YES on Prop. 39 to create a national model for implementing Voter ID in a bipartisan way.

**Margit Whitlock**, Democratic Coalition Chair  
 Californians for Voter ID  
 **Tafa Jefferson**, Republican Coalition Chair  
 Californians for Voter ID  
 **Joe Green**, Independent Coalition Chair  
 Californians for Voter ID

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 39

NO on PROP. 39—Stop Trump from rigging our elections. *Don’t believe the lies.* Prop. 39 MAKES VOTING HARDER, MORE EXPENSIVE, AND LESS SAFE for Californians.

PROP. 39 IS FUNDED BY MAGA RIGHTWING BILLIONAIRES. Follow the money. MAGA billionaires have spent millions spreading election lies. Republican operatives have pushed this voter suppression agenda for years. They want Trump to have unlimited power so they get more tax breaks for the rich while cutting funding to healthcare and schools for the rest of us.

California election officials already verify voters. Prop. 39 just ADDS EXTRA HURDLES for citizens. THE FACTS DON’T LIE. When Texas tried this, they threw out *12 times more mail ballots* than California.

Prop. 39 creates new threats of identity theft. No citizen should have to choose between their privacy and their right to vote.

The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office found that Prop. 39 could COST HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS EACH YEAR—read it for yourself. MAGA extremists want to use your taxpayer dollars to buy Trump an expensive gift: blocking eligible voters and giving the Big Lie a win in California. We won’t fall for it.

PROP. 39 TRIES TO DISTRACT US from how Trump and his billionaire friends have failed Americans. Hospitals are closing. Fire victims are still waiting for help. Groceries and housing costs are more expensive than ever. Now they want to use Prop. 39 to control our elections and avoid accountability.

NO KINGS. NO LIES. NO PROP. 39.

**Alex Padilla**, U.S. Senator for California  
 **Catherine Kennedy**, President  
 California Nurses Association  
 **Adam Weinberger**, President  
 California School Employees Association

### ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 39

*VOTE NO.* Donald Trump lies about elections and uses those lies to grab power.

STOP TRUMP’S POWER GRAB. Trump wants revenge on California—he has delayed LA wildfire relief, undone laws to keep our air and water clean, and constantly attacked our immigrant friends and neighbors. Now he wants to undo our freedoms and democracy with Prop. 39. Trump’s cronies want to rig California elections so they can seize and keep control of Congress and the White House. Trump will do whatever it takes to tear apart our right to vote, dodge accountability, and hold onto authoritarian power.

CALIFORNIANS WON’T FALL FOR IT. We have a chance to fight back and stop Trump by voting NO on Prop. 39. Don’t let California become the next state where politicians pick which voters count.

WASTES HUNDREDS OF MILLIONS OF DOLLARS.

Trump and his accomplices want California to spend *hundreds of millions of dollars* to chase their election lies and conspiracy theories. Californians are struggling, and Trump wants YOU to pay for his conspiracies.

PUTS YOUR IDENTITY AT RISK. Prop. 39 will make every vote by mail voter include their personal details on their return envelope—making voters easy targets for identity theft. Voters would have to choose between voting and protecting their privacy.

BLOCKS CITIZENS FROM VOTING. Prop. 39 adds new hurdles—voters would have to include a personal ID number on their ballot envelope that has to exactly match state records. Get one digit wrong, and a valid ballot could get thrown out. If you don’t take extra steps to tell officials which ID you want to use for voting—you may not get a mail ballot at all. And if the address on your ID is not up to date or your name is misspelled—your vote might be rejected.

PUSHES OUT VOTERS. “Free” state IDs aren’t free: voters still pay for transportation, time off work, and costs like childcare or getting required documents. Seniors, students, low-income workers, voters of color, and the millions of women who changed their names at marriage are hit hardest. These unfair barriers help politicians choose their voters instead of the other way around.

TRUMP LIES TO GRAB POWER. DON’T LET THOSE LIES TAKE AWAY YOUR VOTE.

*PROTECT YOUR VOICE. PROTECT YOUR VOTE. VOTE NO.*

Learn more at *CAforVotingRights.org*

**David Trujillo**, Executive Director  
 ACLU California Action  
 **Darius Kemp**, California State Director  
 Common Cause  
 **Lorrel Plimier**, Co-President  
 League of Women Voters of California

### REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST  
PROPOSITION 39

*PROP. 39 IS BIPARTISAN—NOT ABOUT DONALD TRUMP OR GAVIN NEWSOM*

Prop. 39 gives California a bipartisan solution for election security. While politicians in D.C. fight over partisan control of elections, Californians can adopt our own solution: Voter ID. Opponents will claim this measure is about Donald Trump or Gavin Newsom. It isn’t. Prop. 39 is a California solution to growing mistrust in our elections. Democrats, Republicans, and Nonpartisans encourage you to reject the big-money partisan allegations and vote yes on Prop. 39 to encourage voter participation and protect our elections.

*PROP. 39 IMPROVES ELECTION MANAGEMENT*

Prop. 39 improves the accuracy of our voter lists and requires independent audits to strengthen election management.

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"California Proposition 39 2026 voter ID initiative analysis","content":"**California Proposition 39 (November 3, 2026) is an initiated constitutional amendment that would require government-issued identification for in-person voting and the last four digits of a designated government ID number on mail ballot envelopes, while also mandating citizenship verification efforts on voter rolls.** It qualified for the ballot after supporters submitted over 1.3 million signatures (exceeding the 874,641 required) in early 2026. If passed, it would make California the 37th state requiring voter ID and amend the state constitution, with the Legislature directed to enact implementing details. The official ballot title, revised by Attorney General Rob Bonta, reads: “Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification.” Proponents challenged this as misleading, but a court upheld it.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_39)

### Key Provisions
The measure would change voting procedures as follows:
- **In-person voting**: Voters must present government-issued ID (e.g., driver’s license, passport, or state ID). Those without it would be turned away. The state must provide a free voter identification card upon request, usable for voting.
- **Vote-by-mail (used by ~80-82% of California voters)**: New and existing voters must select a government-issued ID number during registration. They must write the last four digits of that number on the ballot envelope. Officials would match it against registration records; mismatches or missing numbers would invalidate the ballot. Critics note it does not explicitly require a “cure” process (unlike signature mismatches).
- **Citizenship verification**: State and local elections officials must make “best efforts” using government data to verify U.S. citizenship of registered voters and report annually the percentage verified per county.
- **Oversight**: The State Auditor must review state and county compliance every odd-numbered year and make recommendations. The measure is self-executing upon passage but requires legislative action for details like acceptable IDs and “best efforts” standards. Citizens could seek judicial review for non-compliance.[[2]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)

Currently, California (one of 14 states without Election Day ID requirements) verifies identity primarily via signatures: in-person voters sign a poll book, and mail ballots undergo signature matching (with a cure process for mismatches). Registration requires a driver’s license/state ID number or last four SSN digits, plus an attestation of citizenship under penalty of perjury. Non-citizens voting in most elections is already illegal. In November 2024, ~13 million voted by mail and ~3 million in person. Signature mismatches rejected over 100,000 ballots in a recent election, per proponents.[[2]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)

### Fiscal Impact
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates annual state and local costs of **tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars** (less than 0.25% of the General Fund), depending on implementation choices like ID card design, volume requested, and verification processes. Potential savings from fewer registered voters (e.g., removing ineligible ones) would likely not offset costs. Proponents have called the estimate “absurd.”[[2]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)

### Supporters, Opponents, and Funding
**Proponents** (led by Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and Reform California/Californians for Voter ID) include the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, Latino American Political Association, California Women’s Leadership Association, Transparency Foundation, California Republican Party, and some conservative groups. They frame it as a bipartisan, common-sense reform to boost trust, citing polls showing majority support across parties when presented simply. The Yes campaign raised over $36 million, with major donors including Illinois billionaire Richard Uihlein ($17 million), Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia ($8 million), and others like Nicole Shanahan.[[3]](https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39)

**Opponents** include Governor Gavin Newsom, Sen. Alex Padilla, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, ACLU California Action, Common Cause, League of Women Voters of California, major labor unions (e.g., California Teachers Association, SEIU), voting rights groups, and the California Democratic Party (largest opposition donor at ~$6.5 million). They argue it is unnecessary (voter fraud is rare), costly, a form of suppression targeting low-income, minority, elderly, disabled, and name-change voters, and part of a national “Trump agenda.” The No side has raised less but mobilized Democratic infrastructure.[[4]](https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317856630.html)

### Arguments For and Against
**In favor**: It is a bipartisan solution (nearly half of qualifying signatures from Democrats/Independents) that increases election trust and participation without eliminating mail voting or other access features. Signature matching is error-prone and delays results; voter ID in other states with free IDs has not suppressed turnout and may increase it by building confidence. It includes audits and citizenship checks for accurate rolls. Proponents emphasize accessibility via free IDs and existing conveniences.[[5]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)

**Against**: It adds unnecessary barriers that could reject valid ballots (e.g., transcription errors on envelopes, no explicit cure process), risks identity theft by putting ID digits on mail envelopes, and wastes taxpayer money chasing rare in-person impersonation fraud. It disproportionately burdens certain groups and lacks proof of widespread issues. Opponents highlight the partisan funding and title as evidence of a suppression effort. Some analyses note California already has strong verification, and documented fraud is minimal.[[5]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm)

### Polling and Outlook
Polling has been mixed but generally shows the measure trailing or close, with strong partisan divides (Republicans ~90%+ Yes; Democrats ~80% No; Independents split). Early 2026 polls showed majority support in some cases, but later ones (e.g., Berkeley IGS October 2026: 37% Yes/57% No; PPIC: 41% Yes/58% No) indicated opposition leading. Support drops when voters hear both “prevent fraud” and “could disenfranchise” framings. One forecast projected ~45% Yes (likely to fail). It is highly polarized, with Yes leaning Republican. Other states (Nevada, North Carolina, Oklahoma) have similar 2026 measures.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_39)

### Broader Analysis and Potential Effects
This measure imports a national election-integrity debate into California, where mail voting dominates and trust issues persist among some (especially Republicans). Proponents argue it addresses perception problems and signature issues without restricting access. Critics, including voting rights experts, warn of implementation challenges, higher rejection rates (citing Texas examples), privacy risks, and no evidence of outcome-altering fraud. If passed, it would take effect after certification, with the next major elections in 2028; lawsuits over implementation or federal preemption are possible. It would not require proof of citizenship at registration (unlike some federal proposals) and preserves mail voting.

The debate reflects California’s political landscape: a Democratic-leaning state with a Republican-backed initiative funded by out-of-state conservatives, testing voter ID’s appeal amid low documented fraud but declining trust. Outcomes would depend on turnout, messaging, and whether voters prioritize security over access concerns. For the full text, official analysis, and arguments, see the California Secretary of State’s Voter Information Guide.","citations":["https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_California_Proposition_39","https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm","https://www.kqed.org/voterguide/california/proposition-39","https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317856630.html","https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/arguments-rebuttals.htm"],"allowed_domains":null}

The official text of the proposed law (from the California Secretary of State’s Official Voter Information Guide) is as follows:[[2]](https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf)

**PROPOSED LAW**

**SECTION 1. Findings and Purposes.**  
To enforce existing voter qualifications, including US citizenship, established by California’s Constitution, the people hereby amend the California Constitution: (A) to promote public confidence and trust in the electoral process, which encourages civic participation and supports a healthy democracy; (B) to deter and detect voter fraud by maintaining accurate voter registration records and confirming eligibility to vote; and (C) to minimize the risk of voter impersonation by requiring proof of identity to vote.

**SEC. 2. California Voter Identification Reforms.**  
Article II of the California Constitution is amended to add section 3.1 to read as follows:

**SEC. 3.1.**  
(a) The Secretary of State, and county elections officials, shall each have the duty to maintain accurate voter registration lists, shall use best efforts to verify citizenship attestations using government data, and shall annually report what percentage of each county’s voter rolls have been citizenship-verified.

(b) Each time a voter casts a ballot in person in any election in the State, the voter shall present government-issued identification, or if voting by mail, the voter shall provide the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification that matches the one designated by the voter for their voter registration. The type of identification designated by each voter must be indicated in their voter registration record, noted on the mail ballot envelope provided to them, and available to them on request by phone or electronically. Election officials shall only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying the identity of the person voting pursuant to the requirements of this section, and verifying that the person has cast only one ballot in the election. Government-issued identification means documentation that allows conclusive verification of the voter’s identity. Upon request by an eligible voter, the State shall provide, at no charge, a voter ID card for use in casting a ballot.

(c) This section shall be self-executing. The Legislature shall also promptly enact laws to implement this section, provide for voting by military and overseas voters consistent with federal law, and ensure that all State and local officials comply and support the compliance with this section. Citizens may seek judicial review and remedy of the State’s or any county’s compliance with this section. During every odd-numbered year, the California State Auditor shall audit the State’s and each county’s compliance with this section and report its findings and recommendations for improving the integrity of elections to the public.

**SEC. 3. Severability.**  
The provisions of this act are severable. If any portion, section, subdivision, paragraph, clause, sentence, phrase, word, or application of this act is for any reason held to be invalid by a decision of any court of competent jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect the validity of the remaining portions of this act, which shall be given effect without the invalid portion or application.

The full official voter guide (including analysis, arguments, and this text) is available at voterguide.sos.ca.gov. The measure requires additional implementing legislation from the Legislature for details such as qualifying forms of ID. Fiscal estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office project annual state and local costs in the tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars.[[3]](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm)

For the most current official version, refer to the California Secretary of State’s site, as ballot language and titles can be subject to legal challenges.","citations":["https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/quick-reference-guide/39.htm","https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/complete-vig.pdf","https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/39/analysis.htm"],"allowed_domains":null}

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"Texas 2022 mail ballot rejection rate ID number requirement SB1","content":"**In Texas, Senate Bill 1 (SB 1, 2021) added a requirement that mail-in (absentee) voters include a matching ID number—driver’s license/personal ID or last four digits of SSN, matching the one on their voter registration—on both the ballot application and the carrier envelope.** Missing or mismatched numbers led to rejections (with a cure process available). This caused a sharp spike in 2022, especially in the March primary (the first statewide election under the law), followed by a drop in the November general election after voter education, form updates, and familiarity.[[1]](https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2025/05/28/mail-voting-decline-under-senate-bill-1-election-law-id-requirement/)

### 2022 March Primary
- Statewide mail ballot rejection rate: **12.38%** (24,636 rejected out of 198,947 returned). This included ~12,000 rejected applications. Rates were similar by party (~12.9% Democratic, ~11.8% Republican).[[2]](https://www.cbsnews.com/texas/news/exclusive-texas-sec-of-state-john-scott-on-rejected-mail-ballots/)
- Vast majority (~90% or more) of rejections were due to the new SB 1 ID matching requirement (not signatures or other issues). This was far higher than prior years (e.g., ~1% or less in 2020; ~1.7–1.8% in 2018).[[3]](https://www.votebeat.org/texas/2022/10/20/23413651/sb1-mail-ballot-rejections-asian-latino-black-voters/)
- In large counties, rates ranged from ~6% to 22% (e.g., ~19% in Harris County). Many voters (especially those 65+ or with disabilities, who qualify for mail voting) did not successfully vote after rejection. Studies (e.g., Brennan Center) found racial disparities, with higher rates for Asian, Latino, and Black voters than White voters.[[4]](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/records-show-massive-disenfranchisement-and-racial-disparities-2022-texas)

### 2022 November General Election
- Statewide mail ballot rejection rate: **2.7%** (9,348 rejected). This was a major improvement from the primary but still higher than recent midterms (~1.5–1.8%). Preliminary data from large counties showed ~4%.[[5]](https://www.cnhinews.com/cnhi/article_c0fa002e-7d63-11ed-859e-93b2426481b5.html)
- Over 80% of rejections were still tied to SB 1 ID issues. Harris County (largest) had a higher rate (~4.5%). Some analyses (e.g., EAC/Ballotpedia data) report slightly different figures like 3.4% (12,575 rejected), possibly due to methodology or including more categories.[[6]](https://www.houstonchronicle.com/politics/election/2022/article/New-Texas-law-leads-to-10-000-rejected-mail-17577757.php)

The drop from primary to general was attributed by the Texas Secretary of State to education campaigns, redesigned envelopes/inserts, and a statewide tracker. {"type":"WebSearch","query":"voter impersonation fraud rates United States studies Brennan Center Heritage database California","content":"**Voter impersonation fraud (in-person voting while pretending to be another registered voter) is extremely rare in the United States according to multiple studies, with rates typically measured in the range of 0.0003% or far lower.** It has not been shown to affect election outcomes at scale. This holds across Brennan Center analyses, academic work, government reviews, and even the Heritage Foundation's own database of proven cases. ### Brennan Center and Related Studies
The Brennan Center for Justice's 2007 report *The Truth About Voter Fraud* reviewed meticulously studied elections and found impersonation incident rates of 0.0003% to 0.0025%. It concluded that an American is more likely to be struck by lightning than to impersonate another voter at the polls. Most alleged fraud traces to clerical errors, data mismatches, or administrative issues rather than intentional impersonation.[[2]](https://sandersinstitute.org/debunking-the-voter-fraud-myth)

A 2012 News21 (Arizona State University) analysis of 2,068 alleged election-fraud cases nationwide since 2000 found only 10 involving in-person impersonation—about 1 per 15 million registered voters. A follow-up in five states (2012–2016) found zero successful prosecutions for impersonation.[[3]](https://www.mediamatters.org/research/2016/10/21/right-wing-media-figures-conflate-voter-fraud-voter-registration-inaccuracies/214037)

Academic list experiments (e.g., a 2014 *Election Law Journal* study) found no evidence of widespread impersonation even in contested states, with self-reported rates indistinguishable from those for alien abduction. U.S. Department of Justice efforts (2002–2005) and other reviews similarly yielded vanishingly small numbers, with no coordinated impersonation schemes. The Government Accountability Office noted challenges in estimating incidence due to data limitations but highlighted studies showing it as isolated.[[4]](https://johnahlquist.net/files/AhlquistMayerJackmanELJFinal.pdf)

### Heritage Foundation Database
The Heritage Foundation maintains a database of "proven instances" of election fraud (convictions, judicial findings, etc.), described as a sampling rather than comprehensive. Heritage includes impersonation as one category among others like absentee fraud, ineligible voting (felons, noncitizens, deceased), and vote-buying. {"type":"WebSearch","query":"academic evidence voter ID laws effect on turnout meta analysis 2020 2024","content":"**No dedicated meta-analysis of voter ID laws’ effects on turnout was published 2020–2024.** Literature reviews and high-quality causal studies (difference-in-differences, synthetic DiD, matching on administrative voter files) from this period generally find small, null, or heterogeneous effects on overall turnout, often 0–3 percentage points, with debate over subgroup impacts (especially racial/ethnic minorities) and data sources (surveys vs. official records). Effects appear smaller than those of registration barriers and are sometimes offset by party mobilization.[[1]](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-081624-081637)

### Key Reviews and Surveys (2020–2025)
A 2024/2025 survey by Cantoni, Pons, and Schäfer (NBER working paper; *Annual Review of Economics*) reviews (quasi-)experimental evidence on voting procedures. Voter ID laws raise the *cost* of voting (like registration requirements). Obstacles matter more pre-election when stakes are low and less when parties mobilize or alternatives (e.g., mail voting) exist. They note heated U.S. debates but emphasize that many studies find modest effects; they broaden beyond ID/convenience voting to other rules.[[2]](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4957395)

Highton (2017, *Annual Review of Political Science*, frequently cited in later work) concluded modest overall turnout effects with limited differences across groups; later papers build on or critique this. A 2023 UCLA Law Review article (Zhang) argues empiricists detect at most ~2 pp effects because >99% of *registered habitual voters* already have ID (unlike many eligible non-registrants); causal studies of turnout *conditional on registration* were never likely to find large drops.[[3]](https://www.uclalawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/securepdfs/2023/05/Zhang-Final-Article-Pages.pdf)

### Major Empirical Studies, 2020–2024
- **Cantoni & Pons (2021, *Quarterly Journal of Economics*)**: Nationwide panel of 1.6 billion observations (2008–2018 voter files). Strict ID laws had **no negative effect** on registration or turnout overall or by race, gender, age, or party. Most demanding spec: −0.1 pp (95% CI rules out >3 pp drop). Nonwhite turnout relative to White: +1.4 pp (CI includes zero). Increased campaign contact of nonwhites (~4.7–5.4 pp) may have offset modest effects. No effect on fraud. Holds for photo vs. non-photo and midterms vs. presidential.[[4]](https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/136/4/2615/6281042?login=true)

- **Kuk, Hajnal, et al. (2020, *Sociological Perspectives*)**: CPS survey data across nine elections. Strict photo ID reduced self-reported turnout probability by up to 4 pp (enough to swing close races); effects for all racial groups but disproportionately larger for Latinos. Contrasts with admin-data studies; critics note survey measurement error.[[5]](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348036613_The_Suppressive_Impacts_of_Voter_Identification_Requirements)

- **Grimmer & Yoder (2022, *Political Science Research and Methods*)**: North Carolina photo ID (in effect for 2016 primary, then suspended). For the ~3% lacking ID, 0.7 pp turnout drop in the primary vs. those with ID. Effect persisted after repeal (2.6 pp in 2016 general, 1.7 pp in 2018). Precise estimates using matching + DiD on admin data.[[6]](https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/pscirm/v10y2022i3p453-469_1.html)

- **Lipkovitz (2025, *Research & Politics*)**: State-level turnout 1984–2020 + synthetic DiD. **No significant aggregate effect**. Heterogeneity: late-adopting states (post-2008) saw 2.7 pp drop in presidential elections; early adopters unaffected. Midterms showed possible *increase* (not robust). Modest/opposing effects net to near-zero, consistent with small equilibrium impacts of reforms. Robust to 2022/2024 data.[[7]](https://doi.org/10.1177/20531680251401762)

- **UK evidence (post-2022 Elections Act photo ID)**: 2023 English local elections showed 2.1–3.3 pp turnout drop (Oxford/BES studies using pre-post + individual panel data); larger (6.4 pp) among those without ID. 1.2–2.4% of registered voters reported being turned away or deterred. 2024 general election effects smaller (~1.3%). ~5% of voting-age population lacked valid ID, concentrated among poorer/less-educated/left-leaning groups. Electoral Commission: 0.25% turned away at polls. Mixed with some confidence gains.[[8]](https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/133062/html/)

Other 2020–2024 work (e.g., Virginia 2014 law, Rhode Island) finds small drops concentrated among those without ID or via reduced registration, not large overall suppression.

### Overall Picture and Caveats
High-quality admin-data causal studies (Cantoni-Pons, Grimmer-Yoder) find **small/null overall effects**, ruling out large suppression. Survey-based work (Kuk et al.) finds larger/disparate effects, possibly due to overreporting or selection. Heterogeneity by adoption timing, election type, and ID strictness exists. Effects are typically smaller than registration costs and can be offset by mobilization. Most registered voters already possess ID. Claims of massive suppression or zero impact both overstate the evidence. Future work should examine long-run registration effects and non-U.S. contexts.[[9]](https://factually.co/fact-checks/politics/research-turnout-effects-strict-photo-id-vs-non-strict-id-laws-c6ced0)

For full papers, search Google Scholar or NBER/QJE/Annual Reviews. Evidence continues to evolve with new elections and methods.","citations":["https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-economics-081624-081637","https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4957395","https://www.uclalawreview.org/wp-content/uploads/securepdfs/2023/05/Zhang-Final-Article-Pages.pdf","https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/136/4/2615/6281042?login=true","https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348036613_The_Suppressive_Impacts_of_Voter_Identification_Requirements","https://ideas.repec.org/a/cup/pscirm/v10y2022i3p453-469_1.html","https://doi.org/10.1177/20531680251401762","https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/133062/html/","https://factually.co/fact-checks/politics/research-turnout-effects-strict-photo-id-vs-non-strict-id-laws-c6ced0"],"allowed_domains":null}

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"Georgia mail ballot ID number rejection rate 2022 2024 absentee SB202","content":"**Georgia’s overall absentee/mail-in (absentee-by-mail) ballot rejection rates were 1.5% in the 2022 general election and 1.7% in the 2024 general election.** These figures come from analyses of returned ballots (not including applications). SB202 (the 2021 Election Integrity Act) introduced a requirement to provide a Georgia driver’s license/state ID number (or last four SSN digits if none) on the absentee ballot oath envelope, along with other changes like shortened request/return windows. ID-related rejections (incorrect or missing ID information) form a subset of total rejections and were near-zero pre-SB202 because the specific ID-number matching rule was new.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results,_2024:_Analysis_of_rejected_ballots)

### Overall Rejection Rates
- **2022 general**: ~252,272 absentee/mail ballots returned; 3,785 rejected (1.5% rate). This was up from 0.4% in 2020 (pre-SB202 presidential) but down from higher pre-pandemic rates like 3.1% in 2018 in some comparisons.[[2]](https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results%2C_2022:_Analysis_of_rejected_ballots_in_the_2022_general_election)
- **2024 general**: ~273,512 returned; 4,761 rejected (1.7% rate). This was a slight increase from 2022 (+0.2 percentage points) and higher than 2020, though still below some earlier midterm/presidential cycles in certain datasets. Nationwide, 2024 mail rejection was 1.2%. Late receipt (after deadline) was a major driver of the post-SB202 increase, as SB202 tightened timelines.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/Election_results,_2024:_Analysis_of_rejected_ballots)

Mail voting volume dropped sharply post-SB202 (from high 2020 pandemic levels back toward pre-2020 norms, around 5% of ballots in 2024), with larger drops among Black, AAPI, and Latino voters. Racial disparities in usage and some rejection categories persist in expert analyses from ongoing litigation.[[3]](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/georgias-sweeping-anti-voting-law-suppressed-black-votes-new-data-shows/)

### ID Number-Specific Rejections (Incorrect or Missing ID Information)
SB202 requires matching the provided ID number (DL/state ID or last 4 SSN) plus date of birth against voter records. Voters can often “cure” issues. Pre-SB202, this specific matching was not required in the same way, so ID-number rejections were 0% in 2020/Jan 2021 (and 0.12% incorrect + 0.09% missing in 2018).

From expert reports in SB202 litigation (Fraga analysis of state data):
- **2022 (Nov general)**: Incorrect ID information: 0.11%; missing ID information: 0.34%. Combined ID-related ~0.45% of absentee-by-mail ballots. (Dec 2022 runoff: incorrect 0.16%, missing 0.51%.) These were higher than pre-SB202. Other reasons included late receipt (0.84% in Nov 2022) and signatures.[[4]](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.gand.298267/gov.uscourts.gand.298267.810.21.pdf)
- **2024**: Exact ID-number breakdowns are less publicly tabulated in the same format, but expert reports (Fraga, Grimmer, etc.) in the same litigation note that incorrect/missing ID rejections remained higher than pre-SB202 levels. Overall ID + signature issues stayed under 1% of absentee ballots (consistent with trends since 2016). Defendants’ analyses state 99.6% of 2024 absentee applications and ballots complied with SB202 ID rules, with application ID-issue rejections at 0.37%. Plaintiffs highlight racial disparities (higher rates for Black, Latinx, and AAPI voters) and note ID mismatches as one factor alongside late ballots. Total 2024 rejections were ~4,761, with late receipt a larger share than ID issues.[[5]](https://www.democracydocket.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/977-2025-09-12-State-defendants-supplemental-brief-in-support-of-motions-for-summary-judgment.pdf)

ID rejections are a minority of total rejections; late arrival and (to a lesser extent) signatures/oath issues dominate. Cure processes exist, and most ballots are accepted. Data comes primarily from Georgia Secretary of State files analyzed in court (ongoing NAACP et al. v. Raffensperger litigation) and Election Assistance Commission/Ballotpedia compilations. Official county-level or full 2024 reason breakdowns may be available via Georgia SOS absentee files or EAVS reports. {"type":"WebSearch","query":"California noncitizen voter registration proven cases 2020-2026 scale","content":"[[1]](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-06-25/justice-department-sues-orange-county-registrar-to-get-data-from-noncitizen-voting-records)[[2]](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-charges-28-foreign-nationals-california-election-crimes)[[3]](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/la-county-checked-a-sample-of-voters-on-dojs-noncitizen-list-1-in-4-were-born-in-the-u-s/)**Proven cases of noncitizen voter registration in California from 2020–2026 are rare, with a very small scale relative to the state's ~23 million registered voters.** Most documented instances involve lawful permanent residents (green card holders) who registered (sometimes years earlier) and, in some cases, voted; these are typically identified through self-reporting, local investigations, or federal data matching rather than widespread fraud. Convictions remain extremely limited historically, and recent federal actions involve charges (not yet proven in court).[[4]](https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.C7UN99E)

### Documented/Removed Cases
- **Orange County (2020–2025)**: Officials identified and removed 17 noncitizens from voter rolls over five years. These individuals either self-reported they were not citizens or were confirmed ineligible by the district attorney's office (often after receiving mail ballots they should not have gotten). This occurred in a county with ~1.9 million registered voters. The county provided names/dates of birth/addresses to federal officials but redacted sensitive details, leading to a 2025 DOJ lawsuit over records access. No evidence these 17 voted in a way that affected outcomes.[[1]](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-06-25/justice-department-sues-orange-county-registrar-to-get-data-from-noncitizen-voting-records)
- California Secretary of State records do not specifically track or report cancellations due to non-citizenship as a distinct category, and the office has stated it has no data on noncitizen voting or incorrect registrations/removals in some responses. Local jurisdictions handle most list maintenance.[[5]](https://hotair.com/headlines/2026/08/21/california-admits-it-doesnt-track-noncitizens-on-voter-rolls-n3818173)

### 2026 Federal Charges
In October 2026, the DOJ charged 28 lawful permanent residents (all green card holders, not undocumented) across California's four federal districts with crimes including fraudulent voter registration (false claim of U.S. citizenship), unlawful voting by an alien (misdemeanor), and/or false statements on naturalization applications. About 11 were arrested initially; more charges followed (reports of ~12 additional, totaling around 40 in some accounts). These individuals appeared on a federal list of ~20,000 "likely noncitizens." Some registered as early as 2019–2020 and voted in 2020, 2022, and/or 2024 elections (e.g., one Belizean national voted in 2020, twice in 2022, and 2024). Others registered/voted on Election Day 2024. All are presumed innocent; some have pleaded not guilty, and proving intent (vs. misunderstanding rules, such as assuming a Real ID or green card allowed voting) can be challenging. These represent a tiny fraction (~0.0001%) of registered voters.[[2]](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-charges-28-foreign-nationals-california-election-crimes)

The DOJ later referenced additional batches, bringing "likely" flagged records to ~37,000, but this is not proven. The 28+ charged cases are the primary recent "proven" (i.e., charged with evidence like registration forms, voting records, and immigration data) examples tied to 2020–2026 activity.

### Broader Allegations vs. Evidence
Federal data matching (voter rolls vs. immigration databases, with commercial tools and manual review) flagged 20,000+ "likely" noncitizens in 2026 (earlier estimates as high as ~190,000). California officials (including LA County) reviewed samples and found the lists unreliable: ~39% of a 200-person LA sample listed a U.S. birthplace (strong citizenship indicator); many registrations were already canceled/inactive (~43–47%); ~70% had no voting history; and an independent UCLA analysis found ~42% of names not even on current statewide rolls, plus potential false positives for naturalized citizens. California has ~23 million registered voters, so even the 20,000 figure is ~0.09%. Officials noted data issues like outdated files and matching errors.[[3]](https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/la-county-checked-a-sample-of-voters-on-dojs-noncitizen-list-1-in-4-were-born-in-the-u-s/)

Heritage Foundation's voter fraud database (sampling proven cases nationwide) records few California convictions for false registrations overall (~40 since 1982) and only a couple specifically for noncitizen voting over decades. Noncitizen voting is illegal under federal law and described as exceedingly rare by fact-checkers, audits, and researchers; it has not been shown to swing elections. Many cases involve green card holders who may not have understood eligibility (they can legally drive/get IDs but cannot vote in federal elections).[[4]](https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.C7UN99E)

### Context on Registration Process
California uses self-attestation of citizenship under penalty of perjury (no documentary proof required at registration). Automatic "motor voter" at DMV excludes AB 60 (undocumented) licenses from being sent to the Secretary of State. Errors have occurred in the past (e.g., 2018 DMV issues affecting ~23,000 files, mostly party preference or opt-out mistakes, with officials stating no undocumented were registered). Noncitizens who register/vote risk deportation, fines, or prison, which experts say deters most.

In short, while isolated cases exist and federal efforts in 2026 highlighted dozens of charged LPRs with activity dating to 2020, the overall scale of *proven* noncitizen registrations/voting is minuscule. Larger flagged numbers remain unverified allegations with documented inaccuracies. For the latest court outcomes on the 2026 charges, check official DOJ or court records, as cases were pending around the 2026 midterms.","citations":["https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2025-06-25/justice-department-sues-orange-county-registrar-to-get-data-from-noncitizen-voting-records","https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-charges-28-foreign-nationals-california-election-crimes","https://www.democracydocket.com/news-alerts/la-county-checked-a-sample-of-voters-on-dojs-noncitizen-list-1-in-4-were-born-in-the-u-s/","https://factcheck.afp.com/doc.afp.com.C7UN99E","https://hotair.com/headlines/2026/08/21/california-admits-it-doesnt-track-noncitizens-on-voter-rolls-n3818173"],"allowed_domains":null}

{"type":"WebSearch","query":"Proposition 39 California 2026 implementation problems cure process analysis CalMatters PPIC Ballotpedia","content":"**Proposition 39 (November 3, 2026 California ballot) is an initiated constitutional amendment requiring government-issued ID for in-person voting, the last four digits of a designated government-issued ID number on mail ballot envelopes (with matching verification against registration), free state-issued voter ID cards on request, “best efforts” citizenship verification of voter rolls using government data with annual county reporting, State Auditor reviews in odd-numbered years, and legislative implementing laws.** It would supersede current law (including a 2024 ban on local voter ID rules) and is self-executing but leaves many details (e.g., qualifying IDs, “best efforts” definition) to the Legislature. A yes vote requires additional identifying information each time a voter casts a ballot; a no vote keeps signature-based verification.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026))

The measure does not explicitly include a “cure” process for mail ballots missing or mismatched ID digits (unlike existing signature mismatches, where officials notify voters and allow correction within a set window, recently extended digitally). Critics, including election experts, note this could lead to more rejected ballots without notice or a chance to fix simple errors like handwriting issues, forgotten designations, or mismatches—especially since ~82% of California votes are by mail. The constitutional text requires officials to “only count a regular or provisional ballot after verifying” identity per the new rules, with no built-in notification/fix mechanism specified. Implementing legislation could potentially add one, but the measure’s language and private right of action (allowing lawsuits over noncompliance) create uncertainty and litigation risk.[[2]](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-39-voting-id-requirements-voter-guide)

### Implementation Problems
- **Vagueness and need for more laws**: Qualifying IDs, how voters designate/select an ID number at registration (and remember it later), “best efforts” for citizenship checks (no comprehensive U.S. citizen database exists; federal records have errors, name variations, or delays for naturalized citizens), and military/overseas voting details are undefined. The Legislature must “promptly” enact laws; delays or disputes could hinder rollout. Citizenship reports could flag eligible voters erroneously, fueling purges, confusion, or lawsuits.[[3]](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026)
- **Costs and administration**: The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars annually (state/local, <0.25% of General Fund), depending on ID card design/demand, verification systems, and reporting. This includes new cards, data matching, audits, and extra processing—potentially slowing counts (already lengthy due to mail volume and existing signature curing) and diverting resources. No new revenue is provided. Privacy concerns arise from last-four digits on envelopes (identity theft risk).[[3]](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026)
- **Ballot rejection and access**: In-person voters without ID would be turned away (provisionals possible but still require verification). Mail mismatches/missing numbers would invalidate ballots. This adds a layer beyond current registration (DL/SSN last four or assigned number + signature) and could disproportionately affect groups with lower ID rates (e.g., some Latinos, youth, low-income, recent movers, or those with name changes). Studies cited by opponents show voter fraud is extremely rare. Additional verification might not speed counting and could increase rejections.[[4]](https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/prop-39-vote-counting-22468723.php)
- **Other risks**: Private lawsuits over compliance; potential federal preemption issues; implementation timing (effective after certification, so not for 2026 itself).

**Ballotpedia** provides the full proposed constitutional text (new Article II, Section 3.1), ballot title/summary (“Prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification”), fiscal note, supporters (e.g., Reform California, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, some Republicans), opponents (ACLU, Common Cause, League of Women Voters), and background on current law. It notes the measure’s origin (signatures gathered after legislative failures) and a failed lawsuit over the Attorney General’s ballot title.[[1]](https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026))

### Identity Theft Risk
Mail theft is a documented issue, and stolen envelopes can expose personal information. Return envelopes often include the voter’s name, address, signature, and (in these states) last four SSN digits or DL number. Thieves targeting mailboxes, collection boxes, or processing can obtain this data, which is useful for identity theft, account takeover, or fraud. Last four SSN digits are not unique (tens of thousands of people can share the same last four, per SSA reports), but combined with name, address, and signature they become more identifying. Proponents of the ID requirement (including some policy groups) argue it is more reliable than signature matching alone, which can be subjective or forgeable, and that last four SSN/DL data is already in voter files. ### Broader Mail Voting Context
Mail/absentee voting uses multiple safeguards: unique voter-specific barcodes/serial numbers on envelopes, signature or ID matching against records, tracking systems, postmark/receipt deadlines, and separation of ballots from identifying envelopes (often via secrecy sleeves in many states). Ballots are typically non-forwardable, and undeliverable ones are canceled.
